By contrast, agreement was lowest for services involving counseling, guidance, or support that respondents may view as already embedded in routine pharmacy practice or with information easily accessible online.

Agreement was lowest for consultation on safe antibiotic use (23.9%), guidance on wound care (32.1%), and assistance with selection of vitamins or herbal supplements (32.5%). For these services, most respondents did not indicate that out-of-pocket payment would be acceptable.

Importantly, there was substantial heterogeneity in beliefs about payment acceptability even for the most highly endorsed services. In the $20 condition, approximately one-fourth of respondents did not view payment as acceptable for osteoporosis screening, and nearly one-third did not view payment as acceptable for travel-related vaccines or pharmacogenomic results review. This variation appears to reflect service-specific judgments rather than general opposition to out-of-pocket payment: 92.4% of respondents viewed payment as acceptable for some services but not others. Thus, while some pharmacist-provided services received meaningful public support, direct out-ofpocket payment did not receive broad consensus across services, and respondents differed in which services they viewed as appropriate candidates for direct payment. In the sections that follow, we examine which respondents are more likely to view out-of-pocket payment as acceptable and whether trust in pharmacists helps explain this variation.

4.2 Correlates of Public Acceptability

Understanding which respondents are more likely to view out-of-pocket payment as acceptable may help identify barriers to direct patient payment for pharmacist-provided services, as well as populations that may be more receptive to these services. Figure 2 examines whether payment acceptability varied systematically by respondents' background characteristics and trust in community pharmacists. Points show estimated coefficients from linear probability models in which the dependent variable was whether the respondent indicated that payment would be acceptable for a given pharmacist-provided service. Models included service fixed effects and an indicator for payment-framing condition. All heterogeneity results are shown in Table 3. Rate of agreement to pay by service, condition, and gender are illustrated in Supplemental Figure 1.

We found several differences in payment acceptability by respondent characteristics. Older respondents were less likely to indicate that payment would be acceptable. Relative to respondents aged 18-26, respondents aged 50-67 and those older than 67 were approximately 5.4 and 6.5 percentage points less likely, respectively, to indicate that payment would be acceptable (both p<0.05). Estimates for respondents aged 27-34 and 35-49 were smaller and less precise.

We also observed differences by gender and race/ethnicity. Relative to female respondents, males were approximately 4.5 percentage points more likely to indicate that payment would be acceptable (p<0.01). Hispanic respondents were approximately 7.2 percentage points less likely to indicate that payment would be acceptable (p<0.01). We found marginal evidence that Black respondents were more likely to find payment acceptable (4.4 percentage points; p<0.10), but we did not find clear evidence of differences for Asian/Pacific Islander respondents, respondents with a college degree or greater, or respondents who identified as health care professionals.

Finally, we examined the association between trust in pharmacists and payment acceptability. A onestandard-deviation increase in the pharmacist trust index was associated with an approximately 2.6 percentage-point higher probability of indicating that payment would be acceptable (p<0.01). Response means for trust constructs ranged from 4.05 ± 0.86 ("makes me feel at ease") to 4.39 ± 0.66 ("is competent"), indicating high levels of pharmacist trust across all constructs. All means for constructs of trust may be found in Supplemental Table 1.

5. Robustness of Agreement to Pay Results

To assess whether the service-level patterns observed in the quota-matched sample were robust to a distinct recruitment source and respondent population, we replicated the survey in an independent convenience sample of University of California San Diego (UCSD) students. The results are shown in Supplemental Figure 2. Among 218 UCSD respondents, service-level payment-acceptability rates in the $20 condition were strongly correlated with those observed in the quota-matched sample (Pearson r = 0.90; Spearman rho = 0.75). Service-level paymentacceptability rates in the any-payment condition were also positively correlated across samples (Pearson r = 0.75; Spearman rho = 0.68). Additionally, we included a $5 stated-price condition to clarify the unexpected finding that agreement was higher in the $20 stated-price condition than in the any-payment condition. Participants were more likely to indicate that the $5 price was acceptable than the $20 price, suggesting that the difference between the stated-price and any-payment conditions was driven by question wording rather than by higher prices increasing acceptability.

These results suggest that services viewed as more acceptable for direct out-of-pocket payment in the quota-matched sample also tended to be viewed as more acceptable in the UCSD sample. The replication supports the robustness of the main finding that payment acceptability varies meaningfully by service type, despite differences in respondent population and study context.

6. Discussion

From the outset of this study, we surmised that shifting pharmacy services from a no-charge model to an out-of-pocket payment model would have a significant impact on the market. However, an a priori prediction of that impact was not possible. Simple economics suggests that there would be a decrease in demand for services even if a fee should be required [14]. Alternatively, services provided for free may be viewed in the context of a "freemium" [15], a business model where some services are offered for free, but charges are imposed for more specialized services. Yet another possibility, concerns the concept of "A fine is a price," a famous finding where adding fees to services increases rather than decreases their demand by making them more explicit [16]. In a similar vein, we wondered if imposing a fee for services by community pharmacists would result in increased patient participation.

Our survey supports the notion that a portion of the population may be willing to pay out-of-pocket for some services that could be made available at community pharmacies. This may suggest that pharmacies considering a "freemium" business model may be feasible. Under this model, if clients are accustomed to having received services at a community pharmacy for no out-of-pocket costs, evolving to payment being a required model could be considered a natural progression, and the pharmacy could build in additional goodwill. We suspect, however, the concept of "A fine is the price" is a dominant factor.

Gneezy and Rustichini essentially employed a "back door" method to ascertain an unmet need. 15 Our survey was conducted using a "front door" method, i.e., asking the question, if health services were to be offered, would the public have the will to pay out-of-pocket costs. Overall, the current survey supports the idea that a significant portion of society is willing to consider payment for services that can be provided at a community pharmacy. The service receiving the greatest positive response, regardless of gender, was osteoporosis screening. This is important, bearing in mind recommendations that all women over the age of 65 years be screened for osteoporosis, given a prevalence of around 27% in this population. It is also recommended that postmenopausal women younger than 65 undergo screening. The benefit for men is not as robust, given a lower incidence of around 6% [17]. This is significant because the consequences of bone fragility and fracture can be severe. Throughout the world, 9.6 million hip fractures were reported in 2019, mainly in women but with increasing prevalence in men, with high one-year mortality rates (15-30%) [18]. For geriatric females following hip fracture, the following formula has been proposed for the prediction of life expectancy: (100 -Patient Age) ÷ 4 [19]. Clearly, there is significant value in identifying individuals who are at high risk and implementing a treatment plan that is directly accessible in a community setting.

It is beyond our scope to suggest independent business practices, but there are many apparent opportunities for interventions by pharmacists that could dovetail with the services suggested by our study. For example, pharmacists could improve osteoporosis management in the local community [20] [21]. The FRAX® tool has been used to evaluate over 50 million individuals for fracture risk (https://www.fraxplus.org/?lang=En) [22], and measurement of calcaneal (heel) bone density using quantitative ultrasound, as can readily be performed by a pharmacist, correlates with dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry bone density [23].

Of the 27 services queried, counseling regarding antibiotic use was lowest on the list. According to the CDC, 255.9 million outpatient oral antibiotic prescriptions were dispensed in 2024 [24]. The notion of unnecessary antibiotic prescriptions [25], or overprescribing leading to antibiotic resistance [26] [27], is beyond the scope of our discussion. However, given the magnitude of antibiotic distribution, it is reasonable to expect that many of those responding to this survey, as representatives of the public, have participated in some manner with antibiotic usage.

In such settings, a counseling session between the patient and the pharmacist is expected and essential, even if for no other reason, to abide by the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act, a U.S. federal mandate that requires, among other stipulations, that a pharmacist offers to counsel patients [28]. Therefore, it is neither feasible nor ethical to dissociate dispensing from counseling, irrespective of the patient's view on payment acceptability. Thus, the overall cost of dispensing the prescribed drug must be all-inclusive.

Between the most and least desirable services described in the survey that can be offered by community pharmacists, i.e., osteoporosis screening (highly desirable) to antibiotic counseling (less desirable), are 25 remaining services representing business opportunities that could be considered as legally allowable, with consideration that scope of practice varies by jurisdiction and that acceptability does not establish business viability. An advantage here is patient accessibility to the community pharmacist. In addition, this survey and other reports demonstrate that the community pharmacist is well respected and trusted by the public [29]. This is the first and critical step for anyone to delegate their health care to another, and our survey suggests they may be willing to do so.

The willingness and desire to receive such services represents a marketplace that will ultimately serve the public good. As described above, osteoporosis screening would clearly alleviate an unmet need. But in a similar vein, consider travel related vaccines. Perhaps 90 million or more US citizens travel to international destinations every year and based on a survey of about one million travelers reported by Lewin et al., 612,795 travelers received 898,196 doses of travel vaccines [30]. This is clearly a service that falls within the expertise of the community pharmacist, and CDC guidance of vaccination requirements is readily available as is additional training and certification by the American Pharmacists Association [31].

Another notable example is assisting with diabetic foot care. Over 10% of the US population is affected by diabetes, around 15% of those will develop foot ulcers, and around 20% of those will require amputation [32]. Here, the community pharmacist can have an impact on quality of life and health outcomes. On the front line, the community pharmacist has direct access to patients with diabetes. Methods of counseling and promoting foot care health are well within the scope of practice [33] [34]. Our survey indicates that patients would be willing to pay for this service, and it is reasonable to expect that such counseling would lead to improved health and wellbeing.

Naloxone counseling and distribution is yet another clinical service that could be easily rendered in the community pharmacy. With opioid-related deaths of great concern across the United States, pharmacists are wellpositioned to identify potential at-risk patients and caregivers who would benefit from training on the administration of naloxone while destigmatizing the issue and the opioid crisis. According to National Association of Boards of Pharmacy (NABP), pharmacists have become an essential part of the country's strategy to combat the opioid epidemic [35]. Naloxone distribution is a key factor in contributing to a decline in opioid overdose deaths.

Pharmacists remain well positioned to continue outreach efforts, education, and distribution in the pharmacy and the community. This service, having an impact beyond the walls of the community pharmacy, is an investment many respondents were willing to pay. Administration of long-acting injectables (LAI), such as extended-release naltrexone or antipsychotics, was a clinical service that ranked high in fee acceptability. Although this service has been in practice for some time, not all pharmacies offer it due to logistics, increase in training, and variable patient demand. Mooney et al. evaluated patient satisfaction with community pharmacist administered LAI antipsychotics and found patients were satisfied and found it more convenient than other settings [36]. Advantages of LAI administration in the community pharmacy span across many domains including increased access and adherence, improved continuity of care, medication therapy management, decreased stigma and increased acceptance in a familiar setting, and early intervention for missed doses. Overall, patient outcomes are improved with increased access and adherence.

Bustamante et al. reported the need to expand patient access to LAI for substance use disorder in the pharmacy setting as there is scant literature on this clinical service in the community pharmacy [37].

Point-of-care testing (POCT) is another area in which respondents were willing to pay a fee for in the community pharmacy. POCT involves performing rapid diagnostic tests in a convenient setting close to patient care sites without sending samples to an outside lab and may encompass tests for COVID-19, influenza A/B, streptococcus A, and RSV with treatment protocols in many cases. Monitoring for glycosolated hemoglobin (A1c), cholesterol levels, and INRs are other POCT that can be performed in the community pharmacy, depending on the state. Increased access to services, convenience, cost, and patient acceptance improves health outcomes for patients and communities. This service may expand in the future as POCT grows into the pharmacogenomics domain and becomes available for use and interpretation in the community pharmacy [38]. Increased education and training will need to coincide with this expansion, but community pharmacists are well positioned to meet the needs of increased POCT. Additional literature suggests that worldwide, pharmacists face similar challenges in providing services without remuneration [39].

Strengths of the current survey include its large quota-matched sample size. In the U.S., there are approximately 270 million adults over the age of 18. To perform a survey with a desirable 95% confidence level and 3% margin of error, a standard sample size formula produces the requirement of 1067 participants. This is the number of participants we selected for this survey. Naturally, however, to be representative of the entire population, it would be necessary to randomly sample based on proper proportions of individuals who reasonably represent the entire U.S. adult population, particularly regarding age, gender, race and ethnicity, education, income, and geographic distribution. This is not a simple task but, given the relatively large number of survey takers (>300,000) associated with the Prolific instrument, we assumed our resulting data would be adequate to answer the key theories of the work, perhaps with some qualifications.

First, the educational level of survey respondents differed from that of the general U.S. adult population.

Approximately 81.8% of survey respondents reported at least some college education (table 2), compared with approximately 62.7% of U.S. adults aged 18 years and older [40]. Conversely, 18.2% of survey respondents reported a high school education or less, compared with approximately 37.3% of the U.S. adult population. Future research should examine whether educational attainment influences perceptions of pharmacist-provided services and stated payment acceptability. Nonetheless, our survey included representation of a large swath of the U.S.

Another variable that may influence the willingness and ability to pay directly for community pharmacistprovided services is household income. As shown in Supplemental Table 2, in our survey, the proportion of respondents reporting annual household incomes below $30,000, and $75,000-$149,999, closely aligned with national estimates [41]. However, respondents reporting household incomes between $30,000 and $149,999 were overrepresented, whereas those reporting incomes of $150,000 or more were underrepresented. Consequently, when evaluating the generalizability of our findings to the broader U.S. population, the income distribution of our sample needs to be considered.

An especially strong feature of our survey is the geographic representation of the respondents [42]. As shown in Supplemental Table 3, only small differences between our sample versus the population distribution were discerned. Accordingly, we conclude that our sample achieves good geographic coverage.

Similarly, our survey participants show excellent alignment with the US population in terms of sex (male and female) and younger age groups (ages 18-26, 27-34, and 35-49) (see Supplemental Table 4) [43]. Also, the total percentage of respondents in the age group of 50 to over 65 (46%) aligns perfectly with the general population in this age range (45%). However, examination of the more narrowly defined age groups of 50-65 and over 65 shows over representation of 7% and underrepresentation of 6%, respectively. Interestingly, relative to the 18-26 age group, respondents aged 50-67 and those older than 67 were approximately 5.4 and 6.5 percentage points less likely to indicate payment would be acceptable. These percentages are not of sufficient magnitude to change the overall interpretation of this study, but further refinement would be of interest.

Lastly, the percentage of participants identifying as Blacks and Asians closely align with the US population (Supplemental Table 4). Ostensibly, however, Hispanic respondents were underrepresented given that 8% selfidentified in this group whereas the Census specifies 17%. The point is somewhat moot given that our survey treats Hispanic identity as a race category, whereas the Census measures Hispanic origin separately from race. Nonetheless, in our survey, those identifying as Hispanic respondents were approximately 7.2 percentage points less likely to indicate that payment would be acceptable (p<0.01). If interest in this point persists, the matter would not be difficult to resolve in a future survey.

Finally, some potential limitations of our study may be noted. First, although Prolific touts a large number of survey participants (approximately 300,000), recruiting participants through this mechanism rather than random sampling may limit the generalizability of our findings. Second, although we considered asking participants if they themselves would pay for the respective services, knowing ahead of time that many of them personally would not require the respective services hypothetical bias may affect responses, as participants might answer differently when faced with actual payment decisions. Next, although the responses were revealing, the framing of the any-payment condition may have introduced ambiguity, as participants could interpret "any amount" as either some positive payment or an unrestricted amount, which was not the intention. Lastly, even though our survey correlated very well with other surveys that have been designed to assess trust in community pharmacists, since trust was measured after participants evaluated the 27 services, this exposure may have influenced their trust ratings and the observed relationship between trust and payment acceptability.

7. Conclusion

The pharmacist is a highly skilled healthcare professional who plays an integral role in the U.S. healthcare system. Our goal was to query services within the entire potential scope of U.S. pharmacist licensure that would meet the needs of the public and could be offered in the immediate future based on the will of the pharmacist and current business models We surmise that any major shift in the current paradigm of community pharmacy services would likely be influenced by the will of the people and the ability to receive payment for service. Our survey results strongly support the notion that a significant portion of the general population believes that people in need of specific services that could conveniently be provided at a community pharmacy would find such services to be of sufficient value to pay out-of-pocket. Naturally, additional surveys can be constructed and administered to acquire additional evidence to support or dispute this payment model. In our view, however, the next best step would be acquisition of definitive evidence through implementation of pilot projects in select market areas where public health improvements could be realized. Service Description

Teaching how to use a medical device Teaches patients how to properly use a medical device (such as an injection, inhaler, blood sugar monitor, or blood pressure cuff) in a single consultation. Teaching how to give an injection Teaches patients how to safely and correctly give themselves a prescribed injection (such as insulin or epinephrine) in a single consultation. Reviewing personal medical device readings Reviews patients' medical device readings (such as blood sugar readings or blood pressure values) and provides guidance on managing their associated condition in a single consultation. Providing support for healthy lifestyle changes Provides guidance to improve patients' diet, exercise, or weight management in a single consultation.

Providing comprehensive medication management

Reviews all of patients' medications to improve safety and effectiveness and recommends modifications as needed. Assisting with choosing or using hearing aids Assists patients with selecting and properly using their hearing aid in a single consultation.

Managing symptoms of dryness

Evaluates and provides treatment recommendations for patients' symptoms of dryness (such as dry eyes or dry mouth) in a single consultation.

Managing skin symptoms

Evaluates and provides treatment recommendations for patients' skin symptoms (such as rash, eczema, or acne) in a single consultation. Providing first aid advice for minor injuries or illnesses Provides advice and treatment recommendations for patients' minor injuries or illnesses in a single consultation.

Providing personalized vaccine recommendations

Reviews patients' vaccination history, recommends, and provides necessary vaccines in a single consultation. The service fee is charged separately from the cost of the vaccines.

Providing travel-related vaccines

Recommends and administers vaccines needed for patients' travel destinations in a single consultation. The service fee is charged separately from the cost of the vaccines.

Managing menopause symptoms

Evaluates and provides treatment recommendations for patients' menopause symptoms in a single consultation. Providing osteoporosis screening Conducts one-time screening to assess patients' bone strength and risk of osteoporosis. Providing consultation on safe antibiotic use Reviews patients' prescribed antibiotics for appropriateness and explains how to use them safely in a single consultation. Providing age-friendly medication consultation Provides a one-time consultation of medications to ensure they are safe and appropriate based on patients' age. Prescribing naloxone (a medication that can reverse opioid overdose) Prescribes naloxone one time and explains how patients can use it in case of an opioid overdose. The service fee is charged separately from the cost of naloxone.

Prescribing HIV prevention medication

Prescribes a supply of medication that helps prevent HIV infection and explains proper use. The service fee is charged separately from the cost of the medication.

Prescribing birth control pills

Prescribes a supply of birth control pills and explains how patients should use them safely. The service fee is charged separately from the cost of the birth control pills. Prescribing emergency contraception Prescribes one-time emergency contraception and explains when and how it should be taken. The service fee is charged separately from the cost of the emergency contraception. Prescribing preventive antibiotics after a tick bite Prescribes preventive antibiotics and explains how to take them after a tick bite consultation. The service fee is charged separately from the cost of the antibiotics.

Testing for common infections
